subtopics.title: Factorise sum or difference of cubes
subtopics.exposition: An expression of the form x^3+y^3 is a sum of two cubes, and it factorises as (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2). An expression of the form x^3-y^3 is a difference of two cubes, and it factorises as (x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2). The sum and the difference of two cubes are two special results obtained from multiplying a binomial and a trinomial. Expanding (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2) gives x^3-x^2y+xy^2+x^2y-xy^2+y^3, in which the x^2y terms and the xy^2 terms cancel, leaving x^3+y^3. Expanding (x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2) gives x^3+x^2y+xy^2-x^2y-xy^2-y^3, in which the x^2y terms and the xy^2 terms cancel, leaving x^3-y^3. Sum of two cubes: x^3+y^3 = (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2). Difference of two cubes: x^3-y^3 = (x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2). To multiply (x+y) by (x^2-xy+y^2), multiply the trinomial by x and by y and add the two results: x(x^2-xy+y^2)+y(x^2-xy+y^2). To multiply (x-y) by (x^2+xy+y^2), multiply the trinomial by x and by y and subtract the second result from the first: x(x^2+xy+y^2)-y(x^2+xy+y^2). The two basic identities for the sum and difference of two cubes are used to factorise more complex examples. To factorise, first decide whether the expression is a sum or a difference of two cubes, use the matching identity, and then identify x and y. Take the cube root of each term that is a perfect cube; the cube roots give the terms in the first bracket and tell us x and y. For a^3-1, the cube root of a^3 is a and the cube root of 1 is 1, so x=a and y=1. Replace x and y in the factorised form of the identity with the values found; this gives the second bracket. a^3-1 = (a-1)(a^2+a+1), found by putting x=a and y=1 into the difference of two cubes identity. Expand the brackets to check that the expression has been correctly factorised. For x^3+8, the cube root of x^3 is x and the cube root of 8 is 2, so x=x and y=2. x^3+8 = (x+2)(x^2-2x+4), found by putting x=x and y=2 into the sum of two cubes identity.

subtopics.title: Common factor before cubes
subtopics.exposition: When the terms have a common factor, take it out first: 16y^3-432 = 16(y^3-27). After the common factor is taken out, the expression left in the bracket is worked on as a difference (or sum) of two cubes, here y^3-27 as a difference of two cubes. For y^3-27, the cube root of y^3 is y and the cube root of 27 is 3. The common factor stays in front of the factorised bracket: 16(y^3-27) = 16(y-3)(y^2+3y+9). To check, expand the factorised form keeping the common factor 16 outside; it returns the original expression 16y^3-432.

subtopics.title: Factorise cubes with compound terms
subtopics.exposition: When the terms have coefficients and other variables, take the cube root of each whole term: the cube root of 8t^3 is 2t and the cube root of 125p^3 is 5p, so x=2t and y=5p. When x and y are themselves products, replace x with (2t) and y with (5p) inside brackets in the identity: (2t+5p)[(2t)^2-(2t)(5p)+(5p)^2]. 8t^3+125p^3 = (2t+5p)(4t^2-10tp+25p^2).

claims.claim: The sum and the difference of two cubes are two special results obtained from multiplying a binomial and a trinomial.
To multiply (x+y) by (x^2-xy+y^2), multiply the trinomial by x and by y and add the two results: x(x^2-xy+y^2)+y(x^2-xy+y^2).
Expanding (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2) gives x^3-x^2y+xy^2+x^2y-xy^2+y^3, in which the x^2y terms and the xy^2 terms cancel, leaving x^3+y^3.
To multiply (x-y) by (x^2+xy+y^2), multiply the trinomial by x and by y and subtract the second result from the first: x(x^2+xy+y^2)-y(x^2+xy+y^2).
Expanding (x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2) gives x^3+x^2y+xy^2-x^2y-xy^2-y^3, in which the x^2y terms and the xy^2 terms cancel, leaving x^3-y^3.
Sum of two cubes: x^3+y^3 = (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2).
Difference of two cubes: x^3-y^3 = (x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2).
The two basic identities for the sum and difference of two cubes are used to factorise more complex examples.
An expression of the form x^3+y^3 is a sum of two cubes, and it factorises as (x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2).
An expression of the form x^3-y^3 is a difference of two cubes, and it factorises as (x-y)(x^2+xy+y^2).
To factorise, first decide whether the expression is a sum or a difference of two cubes, use the matching identity, and then identify x and y.
Take the cube root of each term that is a perfect cube; the cube roots give the terms in the first bracket and tell us x and y.
For a^3-1, the cube root of a^3 is a and the cube root of 1 is 1, so x=a and y=1.
Replace x and y in the factorised form of the identity with the values found; this gives the second bracket.
a^3-1 = (a-1)(a^2+a+1), found by putting x=a and y=1 into the difference of two cubes identity.
Expand the brackets to check that the expression has been correctly factorised.
For x^3+8, the cube root of x^3 is x and the cube root of 8 is 2, so x=x and y=2.
x^3+8 = (x+2)(x^2-2x+4), found by putting x=x and y=2 into the sum of two cubes identity.
When the terms have a common factor, take it out first: 16y^3-432 = 16(y^3-27).
After the common factor is taken out, the expression left in the bracket is worked on as a difference (or sum) of two cubes, here y^3-27 as a difference of two cubes.
For y^3-27, the cube root of y^3 is y and the cube root of 27 is 3.
The common factor stays in front of the factorised bracket: 16(y^3-27) = 16(y-3)(y^2+3y+9).
To check, expand the factorised form keeping the common factor 16 outside; it returns the original expression 16y^3-432.
When the terms have coefficients and other variables, take the cube root of each whole term: the cube root of 8t^3 is 2t and the cube root of 125p^3 is 5p, so x=2t and y=5p.
When x and y are themselves products, replace x with (2t) and y with (5p) inside brackets in the identity: (2t+5p)[(2t)^2-(2t)(5p)+(5p)^2].
